opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The starting point was a fairly simple observation about standard multi-head attention: each head's query, key, and value projections are learned completely independently. Heads end up working in isolated subspaces, and they only "talk" to each other after the fact, when outputs are concatenated and passed through the output projection. That struck us as a bit wasteful. Many heads learn redundant or highly correlated projections, and there's no mechanism for one head to reuse a useful direction another head has discovered.

So the first half of the idea, the projection mixing, is to let heads share and recombine their projection bases. Instead of each head owning a fully private projection matrix, you have a shared pool of projection components, and each head learns how to mix them. You can think of it as moving from "every head builds its own lens from scratch" to "every head composes its lens from a common set of parts." That gives you better parameter efficiency, and it encourages heads to specialize in how they combine features rather than duplicating the same features over and over.

The second half, the exogenous encodings, came from a worry that mixing alone could collapse things. If every head draws on the same pool and the mixing is driven only by the hidden states themselves, the heads can drift toward similar behavior. So we inject a signal that comes from outside the token representations, meaning information that isn't produced by the residual stream at that layer. That could be positional or structural information, or something like a layer- or head-specific code. Its job is to condition the mixing so that different heads, or the same head at different positions, are pushed toward genuinely different combinations. "Exogenous" really just means the mixing coefficients aren't purely endogenous to the content; something external anchors and diversifies them.

The philosophy behind the whole design is that attention heads should be thought of less as independent experts and more as a coordinated system. They should share representational building blocks where it's efficient and stay diverse where it matters. The mixing gives you the sharing, and the exogenous signal protects the diversity.

Honestly, part of the motivation was also practical. As models scale, the number of heads and the size of the projections grow, and a lot of that capacity looks underused when you probe it. We wanted to know whether a little structure in how projections are formed could recover that capacity without changing the overall shape of the Transformer, so the design could be dropped into existing architectures.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest origin of the idea is a frustration with how attention heads are usually treated as sealed boxes. In a standard transformer, each head gets its own query, key, and value projections, and whatever that head learns, it learns alone. The only place heads talk to each other is the output projection, after the softmax has already happened. So by the time information is shared, a lot of the decision about what to attend to has been made in isolation.

Attention projection mixing is our attempt to let heads coordinate before that point. Instead of projecting the input independently for each head, we form the queries and keys from a learned mixture across heads. One head's projection can borrow structure from another's, so if one head has figured out a useful positional pattern, a neighboring head can lean on it rather than rediscover it. In practice, this behaves a bit like a low-rank shared basis with per-head corrections, and it turns out to be cheap because the mixing happens on the projection matrices, not on the sequence.

The "exogenous encodes" part came from a separate observation. We noticed that a surprising amount of head capacity was being spent on reconstructing information that is already known outside the model: position, segment boundaries, modality tags, even simple metadata about the document. That is wasteful. So we inject those signals directly into the mixing weights, not into the token embeddings. The encodes don't change what the tokens are, they change how the heads are combined for a given context. A head can effectively reconfigure itself depending on whether it is looking at code, prose, or a table, without needing more parameters.

The reason we paired the two is that they fix each other's weaknesses. Mixing alone can over-homogenize the heads, and you lose the diversity that makes multi-head attention work in the first place. Exogenous conditioning on the mixing gives you a principled source of diversity that is tied to real structure in the input rather than random initialization. And conditioning alone, without the mixing, has very little leverage, because there is nothing for the external signal to steer.

If I had to compress it to one sentence: we wanted heads to specialize by negotiation rather than by accident, and to give that negotiation access to facts the model shouldn't have to infer.
